title: Every Door Is Different
question: Why did Imam Malik refuse to abandon his teaching for solitary worship — and what does his answer teach about the different doors of good?
audience: English-speaking viewers worldwide, many of them Muslims in the diaspora, who know the scholars' names but not this exchange; they watch long-form story videos on YouTube.
promise: The viewer can say it back: God divides deeds as He divides provision — every person is opened a different door of good, and the door to tend is one's own.

voice.name: OmniVoice design (male, middle-aged, British, low pitch)

look.mood: Indigo night over Madinah and the mountains; silhouette figures in deep indigo against amber-gold light; the same gold at every door; glass chips and pill subtitles, key phrases in amber.

music.note: The kit library's calmest bed, already used under both test films; laid low (≈ −18 LUFS against the voice) so nine minutes never tires.

facts.claim: Abdullah ibn Abdul Aziz al-'Umari, an ascetic worshipper, wrote to Imam Malik ibn Anas urging him to abandon his teaching circle and withdraw into solitary worship like him.
facts.source: at-Tamhid, Ibn 'Abd al-Barr, Juz 5 hal. 202 — verified on Turath (app.turath.io/book/236?page=2701) for the Entri 2 utas, 12 Nov 2026.

facts.claim: Malik replied that Allah has divided deeds just as He has divided provision: one person is opened the door of prayer but not of fasting, another of charity, another of jihad; and that spreading and teaching knowledge is among the finest of deeds, and he was content with what Allah had opened for him.
facts.source: at-Tamhid, Ibn 'Abd al-Barr, Juz 5 hal. 202 (the meaning of Malik's words, written by Ibn 'Abd al-Barr from memory) — same Turath verification.

facts.claim: Malik closed his reply by saying he did not consider what he was upon to be beneath what al-'Umari was upon, that he hoped both were upon good, and that each of them must be content with what was apportioned to him.
facts.source: at-Tamhid, Ibn 'Abd al-Barr, Juz 5 hal. 202 — same Turath verification.

acts.title: The Letter Arrives
acts.goal: Open on the hook: a letter reaches the greatest scholar of Madinah, and it does not praise him — it tells him to stop teaching and worship alone.

acts.title: The Man in the Mountains
acts.goal: Meet the letter's writer fairly: al-'Umari, a sincere worshipper alone in the mountains, certain his path is the only path.

acts.title: Leave Your Circle
acts.goal: Feel the weight of the demand by seeing what it asks Malik to give up: the circle scattered, the books closed, the hall empty.

acts.title: The Night He Answered
acts.goal: Slow down into Malik's night: he reads, is not angry, looks at his sleeping students, and takes up his pen.

acts.title: Every Door Is Different
acts.goal: The answer, drawn as a mechanism: five doors of the same gold light — prayer, fasting, secret giving, teaching, service — each opened for a different person.

acts.title: The Light Multiplies
acts.goal: Show what Malik chose instead: knowledge spreading lamp from lamp, from student to family to a whole city waking in the dark.

acts.title: Both Upon Good
acts.goal: Land the reply's grace: al-'Umari smiles and returns to his prayers; neither path is beneath the other.

acts.title: Tend Your Door
acts.goal: Turn the story on the viewer over the waking city, then say the ideas once more in one frame before the line to remember.

acts.title: The Line to Remember
acts.goal: End on the poster: the one sentence the viewer keeps, held long enough to read twice.
